03-01.script:
The first of March is St David's Day, and across Wales people pin daffodils and leeks to their coats in honour of their patron saint.

On this day in 1872, President Ulysses Grant signed a law creating Yellowstone, the first national park in the world, a land of geysers, hot springs and wandering bison, set aside for the benefit and enjoyment of the people.

In 1896, in the mountains of Adwa, the Ethiopian army of Emperor Menelik defeated an invading Italian force, and Ethiopia kept its freedom when almost all of Africa had been colonised.

On the same day in 1896, in Paris, the physicist Henri Becquerel found that uranium salts had darkened a photographic plate kept in a dark drawer. He had discovered radioactivity.

And in 1919, in Seoul, a declaration of independence was read aloud, and people poured into the streets crying Manse! Korea remembers that brave and peaceful uprising today.

03-02.script:
On the second of March in 1836, in a cold, unfinished building at Washington-on-the-Brazos, delegates signed a declaration making Texas an independent republic. Just a few days' ride away, the defenders of the Alamo were still holding out.

On this day in 1904, Theodor Seuss Geisel was born in Massachusetts. As Dr. Seuss, he gave the world the Cat in the Hat, the Grinch, and Green Eggs and Ham. Schools across America celebrate his birthday by reading aloud.

In 1933, a giant ape climbed the Empire State Building on cinema screens in New York, and King Kong became a legend.

In 1949, an American bomber called Lucky Lady II landed in Texas, after flying all the way around the world without stopping, refuelled four times in the air.

And in 1969, in Toulouse, a slender white aircraft with a drooping nose lifted off for the first time. Concorde would one day carry passengers across the Atlantic in under three and a half hours.

03-03.script:
On the third of March, families in Japan celebrate Hinamatsuri, the Doll Festival. They set out dolls of an emperor and empress and their court on steps covered in red cloth, and wish their daughters health and happiness.

On this day in 1847, in Edinburgh, Alexander Graham Bell was born. He grew up teaching deaf children to speak, and invented the telephone.

In 1861, Tsar Alexander the Second freed Russia's serfs, more than twenty million people who had been bound to the land and its owners.

In 1875, in Paris, the opera Carmen was performed for the first time. The audience was shocked by its fiery gypsy heroine. Today it is one of the most performed operas in the world.

In 1923, the first issue of Time magazine appeared. And in 1931, America adopted The Star-Spangled Banner as its national anthem.

Today is also World Wildlife Day, a day to remember every creature we share this planet with.

03-04.script:
On the fourth of March in 1678, in Venice, Antonio Vivaldi was born. Because of his red hair he was called the Red Priest, and his Four Seasons still bring spring, summer, autumn and winter into concert halls everywhere.

In 1789, the new Congress of the United States met for the first time, in New York, under the Constitution that still governs the country.

In 1877, in Moscow, a new ballet by Tchaikovsky was performed: Swan Lake. Its first reception was lukewarm. Now it is perhaps the most famous ballet of all.

In 1890, the great red Forth Bridge in Scotland opened, a giant of steel cantilevers that still carries trains across the water.

In 1933, in the depths of the Depression, Franklin Roosevelt told a frightened nation that the only thing we have to fear is fear itself.

And in 1979, pictures from Voyager 1 revealed something unexpected: Jupiter has rings, thin and faint, circling the giant planet.

03-05.script:
On the fifth of March in 1770, on a snowy evening in Boston, a crowd jeered and threw snowballs at a line of British soldiers. Shots rang out, and five people lay dead. The Boston Massacre would help turn the American colonies towards revolution.

In 1931, Mahatma Gandhi and the Viceroy, Lord Irwin, signed a pact that freed thousands of prisoners from the Salt March.

In 1946, at a small college in Fulton, Missouri, Winston Churchill warned that an iron curtain had descended across Europe. The words named the Cold War.

Seven years later, in 1953, Joseph Stalin died, and the Soviet Union held its breath.

And in 1960, a photographer named Alberto Korda snapped a picture of Che Guevara at a memorial service in Havana: a beret, a star, a distant gaze. It became one of the most reproduced photographs in history.

In Cornwall, today is St Piran's Day, honouring the patron saint of the tin miners.

03-06.script:
On the sixth of March in 1957, at midnight, before a vast crowd in Accra, Kwame Nkrumah declared that the Gold Coast was free, and would now be called Ghana. It was the first colony south of the Sahara to win its independence, and it lit a flame across the continent.

In 1475, in a village in Tuscany, Michelangelo Buonarroti was born. He would carve David from a block of marble that other sculptors had given up on, and paint the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel.

In 1836, after thirteen days of siege, Mexican troops stormed the Alamo in San Antonio. All of its defenders, including Davy Crockett and Jim Bowie, were killed.

In 1869, a Russian chemist named Dmitri Mendeleev presented his periodic table, arranging all the known elements in rows and columns, and leaving gaps for those yet to be found.

And in 1899, Bayer registered a new name for a medicine made from willow bark: Aspirin.

03-07.script:
On the seventh of March in 1876, Alexander Graham Bell received his patent for the telephone, one of the most valuable patents ever granted.

In 1912, a ship docked in Hobart, Tasmania, and Roald Amundsen hurried to the telegraph office. He sent word to the world: the Norwegians had reached the South Pole.

In 1936, German soldiers marched into the Rhineland, breaking the peace treaties. No one stopped them.

In 1965, six hundred peaceful marchers set out from Selma, Alabama, to walk to the state capital to demand the right to vote. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge, police attacked them with clubs and tear gas. The world saw it on television, and Bloody Sunday changed America.

And in 1971, before a sea of people at the Ramna Race Course in Dhaka, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman gave a speech that stirred a nation. This time, he said, the struggle is for our freedom. Within weeks, Bangladesh would declare its independence.

03-08.script:
The eighth of March is International Women's Day, a day to celebrate women's achievements and to remember how far the fight for equality still has to go.

The day has a remarkable history. On the eighth of March in 1917, women textile workers in Petrograd walked out of their factories, demanding bread and peace. Others joined them, the strike spread, and within a week the Russian tsar had given up his throne.

In 1618, Johannes Kepler found the third of his laws of planetary motion, revealing a beautiful harmony between how far a planet lies from the Sun and how long it takes to circle it.

In 1910, a Frenchwoman named Raymonde de Laroche became the first woman in the world to earn a pilot's licence.

And in 1971, in New York's Madison Square Garden, two undefeated champions, Muhammad Ali and Joe Frazier, met in the Fight of the Century. Frazier won, and the world talked of nothing else.

03-09.script:
On the ninth of March in 1500, a fleet of thirteen ships left Lisbon under Pedro Álvares Cabral, bound for India. Sailing wide into the Atlantic, they found a green coast no European had seen. They had reached Brazil.

In 1796, a young general named Napoleon Bonaparte married a widow named Joséphine, two days before leaving to command the army in Italy.

In 1862, two strange iron ships, the Monitor and the Virginia, fought for hours off the coast of Virginia. Neither could sink the other, but the age of wooden warships was over.

In 1934, in a small village near Moscow, Yuri Gagarin was born. He would become the first human to see the Earth from space.

And in 1959, at a toy fair in New York, a doll named Barbie appeared for the first time, in a black-and-white striped swimsuit. She would become the best-selling doll in the world.

03-10.script:
On the tenth of March in 1876, in a Boston boarding house, Alexander Graham Bell spoke into his new invention: Mr. Watson, come here, I want to see you. In the next room, his assistant heard every word. It was the first telephone call.

In 1831, King Louis-Philippe of France founded the French Foreign Legion, a corps of soldiers from many nations who would become legendary.

In 1913, Harriet Tubman died in New York. She had escaped slavery, then returned again and again to lead others to freedom along the Underground Railroad, and never lost a single passenger.

In 1959, thousands of Tibetans surrounded the palace of the Dalai Lama in Lhasa to protect him, and an uprising against Chinese rule began.

And in 1977, astronomers watching a star pass behind Uranus saw it blink, again and again. They had discovered that Uranus, too, has rings.

03-11.script:
On the eleventh of March in 1702, the first daily newspaper in English, the Daily Courant, appeared in London. It was a single sheet, and promised to give only the news, leaving readers to make up their own minds.

In 1888, a great blizzard buried the east coast of America. Snow drifts rose higher than houses, and New York was cut off for days.

In 1941, President Roosevelt signed the Lend-Lease Act, sending ships, planes and food to Britain, which stood almost alone against Hitler.

In 1990, Lithuania became the first Soviet republic to declare its independence. The empire had begun to come apart.

And in 2011, the largest earthquake ever recorded in Japan struck beneath the sea, and a tsunami swept over the coast, damaging the Fukushima nuclear power plant. More than eighteen thousand people were lost. Each year on this day, Japan remembers in silence.

03-12.script:
On the twelfth of March in 1930, Mahatma Gandhi set out from his ashram near Ahmedabad with seventy-eight followers, walking towards the sea. It was a protest against the British tax on salt. Day after day, crowds joined him. Twenty-four days and almost four hundred kilometres later, at Dandi, he bent down and picked up a lump of natural salt. The world was watching.

In 1912, in Savannah, Georgia, Juliette Gordon Low gathered eighteen girls for the first meeting of what would become the Girl Scouts.

In 1933, Franklin Roosevelt spoke to Americans over the radio from the White House, calmly explaining the banking crisis. It was the first of his fireside chats.

And in 1989, at the CERN laboratory in Switzerland, a young scientist named Tim Berners-Lee handed his boss a proposal for sharing information between computers. His boss wrote on it: vague, but exciting. It would become the World Wide Web.

03-13.script:
On the thirteenth of March in 1781, in the back garden of his house in Bath, a musician and amateur astronomer named William Herschel was scanning the sky with a telescope he had built himself. He noticed a small disc that was not a star. At first he thought it was a comet. It was a new planet, the first discovered since ancient times. We call it Uranus.

On the very same date in 1930, the discovery of another distant world was announced to the world: Pluto, found weeks before by Clyde Tombaugh at the Lowell Observatory. The date was chosen because it was the birthday of Percival Lowell, the observatory's founder, and the anniversary of Uranus's discovery.

In 1881, Tsar Alexander the Second, who had freed Russia's serfs, was killed by a bomb in St Petersburg.

And in 2013, white smoke rose above the Sistine Chapel, and Jorge Mario Bergoglio of Argentina stepped onto the balcony as Pope Francis, the first pope from the Americas.

03-14.script:
The fourteenth of March is Pi Day, because the date, written the American way as three, fourteen, matches the first digits of pi, the endless number that links a circle to its width. Mathematicians celebrate with pies.

Fittingly, on this day in 1879, in the German city of Ulm, Albert Einstein was born. As a boy he wondered what it would be like to ride alongside a beam of light. That question led him to relativity.

In 1794, Eli Whitney received a patent for his cotton gin, a machine that pulled seeds from cotton far faster than any hand.

In 1885, Gilbert and Sullivan's comic opera The Mikado opened in London, and audiences laughed until they cried.

In 1986, the European probe Giotto flew straight into the glowing head of Halley's Comet and photographed its dark nucleus.

And in 2018, on Pi Day and Einstein's birthday, the physicist Stephen Hawking died in Cambridge. He had spent his life explaining black holes and the beginning of time.

03-15.script:
The fifteenth of March is the Ides of March. On this day in 44 BC, Julius Caesar walked into the Senate in Rome, though a seer had warned him to beware this day. He was stabbed by men he had trusted.

In 1493, Christopher Columbus sailed back into the harbour of Palos in Spain, returning from his first voyage across the Atlantic with news of lands no European had known.

In 1848, a young poet named Sándor Petőfi stood on the steps of the National Museum in Pest and read his National Song to the crowd. The Hungarian Revolution had begun, and Hungarians still wear red, white and green cockades today.

In 1917, Tsar Nicholas the Second gave up his throne, ending three centuries of the Romanov dynasty.

And in 1972, The Godfather opened in cinemas. It was, as Don Corleone might say, an offer audiences couldn't refuse.

03-16.script:
On the sixteenth of March in 1926, on a snowy cabbage farm in Auburn, Massachusetts, a quiet physics professor named Robert Goddard lit the fuse of a strange contraption of pipes and tanks. It rose with a roar, flew for about two and a half seconds, and landed in the cabbages. It was the world's first liquid-fuelled rocket, the great-grandparent of every spacecraft that followed.

In 1521, Ferdinand Magellan's battered fleet, having crossed the vast Pacific, reached the islands we now call the Philippines.

In 1850, Nathaniel Hawthorne published The Scarlet Letter, the story of Hester Prynne and the letter A she was made to wear.

In 1867, a Glasgow surgeon named Joseph Lister published his discovery that carbolic acid could keep wounds free of infection. Surgery would become far safer.

And in 1966, Neil Armstrong and David Scott guided Gemini 8 to the first docking of two spacecraft in orbit. Moments later, a stuck thruster sent them spinning, and Armstrong's cool hands brought them safely home.

03-17.script:
On the seventeenth of March, the world turns green for Saint Patrick, the patron saint of Ireland. Legend says he used the three leaves of a shamrock to explain his faith. Today, rivers are dyed green and parades fill the streets of cities from Dublin to Chicago. The first recorded St Patrick's Day parade in New York took place in 1762.

In 1776, after George Washington placed cannon on the hills above the city, the British army sailed away from Boston, and Bostonians still celebrate Evacuation Day.

In 1861, the Kingdom of Italy was proclaimed, uniting a peninsula of many states under one king.

In 1958, America launched Vanguard 1, a little satellite the size of a grapefruit. It still circles the Earth today, the oldest human-made object in orbit.

And in 1973, a photographer at an air base in California captured a returning prisoner of war being greeted by his family, his daughter running towards him with open arms. The picture was called Burst of Joy.

03-18.script:
On the eighteenth of March in 1965, a Soviet cosmonaut named Alexei Leonov opened a hatch and floated out into space, the first person ever to do so. For twelve minutes he drifted on his tether above the turning Earth. Then he found that his suit had swelled so much he could not get back in. Calmly, he let out some air, squeezed through, and lived to paint pictures of what he had seen.

Three hundred years earlier, in 1662, Paris saw the first public bus service, horse-drawn carriages running on fixed routes for a small fare. The idea came from the mathematician Blaise Pascal.

In 1871, the people of Paris rose up and formed the Paris Commune, ruling their city for two months.

In 1922, a British judge sentenced Mahatma Gandhi to six years in prison. Gandhi pleaded guilty and asked for the highest penalty.

And in 1990, thieves dressed as police officers walked into the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston and stole thirteen works of art, including a Vermeer and three Rembrandts. Their empty frames still hang on the walls, waiting.

NASA's MESSENGER becomes the first spacecraft to orbit Mercury.

births.text: Rudolf Diesel, German inventor of the diesel engine
Queen Latifah, American rapper and actress

facts.text: Alexei Leonov's spacesuit ballooned in space, so he let out air to squeeze back into his capsule.
The empty frames of the stolen Gardner Museum paintings still hang on the walls.

03-19.script:
On the nineteenth of March, it is said, the swallows return to the old mission of San Juan Capistrano in California, every year, on St Joseph's Day. People gather to watch for them.

In 1279, at Yamen off the coast of southern China, the last fleet of the Song dynasty was destroyed by the Mongols. The young emperor's minister took the boy in his arms and leapt into the sea. China would be ruled by Kublai Khan.

In 1813, in a Scottish mill town, David Livingstone was born. He would walk across Africa, and become one of the most famous explorers who ever lived.

In 1895, in Lyon, the Lumière brothers set up their camera outside their factory gates and filmed the workers streaming out at the end of the day. It became one of the first motion pictures ever shown.

And in 1932, after eight years of building, the great steel arch of the Sydney Harbour Bridge opened. Before the official ribbon could be cut, a man on horseback galloped forward and slashed it with his sword.

events.text: The Mongols defeat the last Song dynasty fleet at the Battle of Yamen.
Thieves carry out one of the first bank robberies in the United States, in New York.
The Lumière brothers film Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory.
The U.S. Congress establishes time zones and daylight saving time.
The U.S. Senate rejects the Treaty of Versailles.
The Sydney Harbour Bridge opens.
German forces occupy Hungary.
The Academy Awards are televised for the first time.
The Great St Bernard Tunnel opens beneath the Alps.
Argentine scrap-metal workers land on South Georgia, prelude to the Falklands War.
A gamma-ray burst 7.5 billion light-years away is briefly visible to the naked eye.

facts.text: Swallows are said to return to Mission San Juan Capistrano in California every year on St Joseph's Day.

03-20.script:
Around the twentieth of March, day and night are almost equal all over the world. It is the spring equinox in the north, and for millions of people from Iran to Central Asia, the moment the Sun crosses the equator is Nowruz, the New Day, the start of a new year, celebrated with fresh green sprouts, painted eggs and visits to family.

On this day in 1800, Alessandro Volta wrote a letter describing a pile of copper and zinc discs separated by salty cloth that produced a steady electric current. He had invented the battery.

In 1852, Harriet Beecher Stowe published Uncle Tom's Cabin, a novel that stirred millions against slavery.

In 1916, Albert Einstein published his complete theory of general relativity, explaining that gravity is the bending of space and time.

And in 1999, a balloon called Breitling Orbiter 3 crossed the finish line over Africa, completing the first non-stop flight around the world by balloon, nineteen days after it set off from the Swiss Alps.

events.text: The Dutch East India Company is founded.
Alessandro Volta describes his electric battery.
Napoleon returns to Paris, beginning his Hundred Days.
Harriet Beecher Stowe's Uncle Tom's Cabin is published.
Albert Einstein publishes his general theory of relativity.
Tunisia gains independence from France.
John Lennon marries Yoko Ono in Gibraltar.
A gunman tries to kidnap Princess Anne in London.
AZT is approved as the first drug to treat HIV.
A sarin gas attack strikes the Tokyo subway.
Breitling Orbiter 3 completes the first non-stop balloon flight around the world.
The U.S.-led invasion of Iraq begins.

births.text: Sister Rosetta Tharpe, American gospel singer and guitarist

facts.text: Nowruz, the Persian New Year, begins at the exact moment of the spring equinox.
World Sparrow Day began in India in 2010 to help protect the vanishing house sparrow.

03-21.script:
On the twenty-first of March in 1685, in the German town of Eisenach, Johann Sebastian Bach was born into a family of musicians. He would write more than a thousand works, and many still call him the greatest composer of all.

In 1935, the Shah of Persia asked the world to call his country by the name its own people had always used: Iran.

In 1960, at Sharpeville in South Africa, police opened fire on a crowd protesting against the pass laws, and sixty-nine people were killed. South Africans now mark this day as Human Rights Day.

In 1963, the last prisoners left Alcatraz, the island prison in San Francisco Bay.

And in 2006, a young programmer named Jack Dorsey typed a short message on a new service called twttr: just setting up my twttr. It was the first tweet.

Today is also World Poetry Day, a fine day to read a poem aloud to someone you love.

events.text: Germany launches its Spring Offensive on the Western Front.
Tennessee bans the teaching of evolution with the Butler Act.
Persia is officially renamed Iran.
The Moondog Coronation Ball in Cleveland is called the first rock and roll concert.
Police kill 69 protesters at Sharpeville, South Africa.
Alcatraz prison closes.
Martin Luther King Jr. leads the march from Selma to Montgomery.
NASA launches Ranger 9 to photograph the Moon.
San Francisco's mayor proclaims the first Earth Day.
Namibia gains independence.
Jack Dorsey sends the first tweet.

facts.text: The first tweet, by Jack Dorsey, read "just setting up my twttr".
South Africa's Human Rights Day remembers the 69 people killed at Sharpeville in 1960.

03-22.script:
On the twenty-second of March in 1765, the British Parliament passed the Stamp Act, taxing every newspaper, legal paper and playing card in the American colonies. No taxation without representation, the colonists cried, and the road to revolution grew shorter.

In 1873, Puerto Rico abolished slavery, and the island still celebrates its Emancipation Day.

In 1895, in Paris, the Lumière brothers showed their first moving picture to a small private audience. The cinema was about to be born.

In 1912, Bihar was separated from Bengal as a province of its own, and Biharis celebrate Bihar Diwas today.

In 1997, the comet Hale-Bopp made its closest approach to Earth. For months it hung in the evening sky, its two tails glowing, one of the most widely seen comets in history.

And in 1995, cosmonaut Valeri Polyakov returned to Earth after four hundred and thirty-seven days aboard the Mir space station, the longest single journey in space ever made.

events.text: Anne Hutchinson is banished from the Massachusetts Bay Colony.
Britain passes the Stamp Act, taxing the American colonies.
Slavery is abolished in Puerto Rico.
The Lumière brothers give their first private film screening.
Bihar becomes a province separate from Bengal.
President Roosevelt legalises beer, an early step towards ending Prohibition.
The Arab League is founded in Cairo.
Arthur Schawlow and Charles Townes receive the first patent for the laser.
The U.S. Congress passes the Equal Rights Amendment.
Intel ships the first Pentium processor.
Valeri Polyakov returns after 437 days in space, still the longest single spaceflight.
Comet Hale-Bopp makes its closest approach to Earth.

facts.text: World Water Day was first held in 1993.

03-23.script:
On the twenty-third of March in 1775, in a church in Richmond, Virginia, Patrick Henry rose to urge his fellow colonists to take up arms. I know not what course others may take, he said, but as for me, give me liberty, or give me death!

In 1857, in a department store in New York, Elisha Otis installed the first safe passenger elevator. Cities could now grow upwards.

In 1931, in Lahore jail, three young revolutionaries, Bhagat Singh, Rajguru and Sukhdev, were hanged by the British. Bhagat Singh was just twenty-three. India remembers them today as martyrs.

On this same date in 1940, at a great gathering in Lahore, the Muslim League passed a resolution calling for a separate homeland. Pakistan celebrates Pakistan Day in its memory.

And in 1839, a Boston newspaper printed a joke abbreviation, o.k., for oll korrect. It caught on, and today OK may be the most widely used word on Earth.

events.text: Patrick Henry declares: "Give me liberty, or give me death!"
The abbreviation "OK" first appears in print, in a Boston newspaper.
Elisha Otis installs the first safe passenger elevator, in New York.
The University of California is founded.
The Wright brothers apply for a patent on their flying machine.
Benito Mussolini founds the Fascist movement in Milan.

The Enabling Act gives Adolf Hitler dictatorial powers.
The Muslim League passes the Lahore Resolution.
Gemini 3 carries the first two-person American crew into space.
The Pope and the Archbishop of Canterbury meet officially for the first time in 400 years.
Two chemists claim to have achieved cold fusion.
The Mir space station is brought down into the Pacific Ocean.

births.text: Ram Manohar Lohia, Indian socialist leader

facts.text: "OK" began as a joke abbreviation of "oll korrect" in a Boston newspaper.
World Meteorological Day marks the founding of the World Meteorological Organization in 1950.

names: Day of Remembrance for Truth and Justice (Argentina)
03-24.script:
On the twenty-fourth of March in 1882, in a crowded room in Berlin, the scientist Robert Koch announced that he had found the germ that causes tuberculosis, a disease that was killing one in seven people in Europe. The room fell silent. The world now marks this day as World Tuberculosis Day.

In 1603, Queen Elizabeth the First died at Richmond Palace, and a rider galloped north to tell James of Scotland that he was now King of England too.

In 1944, on a moonless night, seventy-six Allied prisoners crawled through a tunnel they had secretly dug beneath Stalag Luft the Third. The Great Escape became a legend.

In 1958, Elvis Presley reported for duty in the U.S. Army, and his famous hair was cut short.

And in 1989, the oil tanker Exxon Valdez struck a reef in Prince William Sound, Alaska, and millions of gallons of oil spilled into the cold, clear water.

events.text: Elizabeth I dies; James VI of Scotland becomes King of England.
Robert Koch announces the discovery of the tuberculosis bacterium.
Alexander Popov demonstrates radio by sending a message between two buildings.
Construction of the New York City Subway begins.
The Tydings–McDuffie Act promises the Philippines independence.
Seventy-six prisoners escape from Stalag Luft III in the Great Escape.
Elvis Presley is inducted into the U.S. Army.
A military coup overthrows Argentina's government.
Morarji Desai becomes Prime Minister of India.
The Exxon Valdez spills oil in Alaska.
Astronomers discover Comet Shoemaker–Levy 9, which will crash into Jupiter.
NATO begins bombing Yugoslavia over Kosovo.

facts.text: The Great Escape tunnel, nicknamed "Harry", was more than 100 metres long.

names: International Day of Remembrance of the Victims of Slavery
03-25.script:
The twenty-fifth of March is Lady Day, the Feast of the Annunciation. For centuries, it was New Year's Day in England.

In 1655, a Dutch astronomer named Christiaan Huygens turned his telescope to Saturn and discovered its largest moon, Titan.

In 1807, the British Parliament abolished the slave trade, after twenty years of campaigning by William Wilberforce and many others. Today the world remembers the millions of victims of slavery.

In 1821, the Greek War of Independence began, and Greeks celebrate their national day with parades of blue and white.

In 1911, fire broke out in the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory in New York. The doors had been locked, and one hundred and forty-six workers, mostly young immigrant women, died. Their deaths led to new laws to keep workers safe.

And in 1957, six nations signed the Treaty of Rome, creating the European Economic Community, the seed of today's European Union.

events.text: Robert the Bruce is crowned King of Scots.
English settlers arrive to found the colony of Maryland.
Christiaan Huygens discovers Titan, Saturn's largest moon.
Britain abolishes the slave trade.
The Swansea and Mumbles Railway carries the world's first fare-paying railway passengers.
The Greek War of Independence begins.
The Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire kills 146 workers in New York.
Greece becomes a republic.
The Scottsboro Boys are arrested in Alabama.
RCA begins making colour television sets.
The Treaty of Rome creates the European Economic Community.
Ward Cunningham launches WikiWikiWeb, the first wiki.

births.text: Norman Borlaug, American agronomist (the Green Revolution)

facts.text: Lady Day, 25 March, was New Year's Day in England until 1752.

03-26.script:
On the twenty-sixth of March in 1971, Bangladesh declared its independence. Nine months of war followed, and a new nation was born. Today Bangladeshis lay flowers at the National Martyrs' Memorial and celebrate their freedom.

In 1484, William Caxton, England's first printer, published Aesop's Fables, the tortoise and the hare, and the fox and the grapes, for English readers.

In 1953, Jonas Salk spoke on national radio to announce that he had tested a vaccine against polio. Asked later who owned the patent, he answered: the people. Could you patent the sun?

In 1979, on the lawn of the White House, Anwar Sadat of Egypt and Menachem Begin of Israel shook hands and signed a peace treaty, ending thirty years of war between their nations.

And in 2012, the film director James Cameron squeezed into a narrow green submarine and dived alone to the bottom of the Challenger Deep, nearly eleven kilometres down, the deepest place in the ocean.

events.text: William Caxton prints Aesop's Fables in English.
An earthquake destroys much of Caracas, Venezuela.
The Book of Mormon is published.
British forces fight the First Battle of Gaza.
The Battle of Iwo Jima ends.
Jonas Salk announces his successful polio vaccine.
Bangladesh declares independence.
Egypt and Israel sign a peace treaty at the White House.
Argentina, Brazil, Paraguay and Uruguay create Mercosur.
The Schengen Agreement removes border checks between seven European countries.
James Cameron makes a solo dive to the Challenger Deep.

facts.text: Purple Day was started in 2008 by a Canadian girl, Cassidy Megan, to raise awareness of epilepsy.
Asked who owned the patent on his polio vaccine, Jonas Salk replied: "Could you patent the sun?"

03-27.script:
On the twenty-seventh of March in 1513, the Spanish explorer Juan Ponce de León sighted a coast full of flowers. Because it was the Easter season, the Feast of Flowers, he named it La Florida.

In 1884, a voice travelled down a wire from Boston to New York, three hundred kilometres, in the first long-distance telephone call.

In 1899, Guglielmo Marconi sent a wireless message across the English Channel, from England to France, without any wire at all.

In 1912, the first lady of the United States, Helen Taft, and the wife of the Japanese ambassador planted two cherry trees beside the Tidal Basin in Washington, a gift from the city of Tokyo. Every spring, millions come to see them blossom.

In 1964, the most powerful earthquake ever recorded in North America shook Alaska for four and a half minutes.

And in 1968, Yuri Gagarin, the first human in space, died in a training flight. He was only thirty-four.

Today is World Theatre Day. The lights go down, the curtain rises, and the story begins.

events.text: Juan Ponce de León sights Florida.
The U.S. Navy is created.
Andrew Jackson's forces defeat the Creek at the Battle of Horseshoe Bend.
Abraham Gesner patents kerosene.
Scotland and England play the first international rugby match.
The first long-distance telephone call is made, between Boston and New York.
Marconi sends the first wireless message across the English Channel.
Japan's gift of cherry trees is planted in Washington, D.C.
Typhoid Mary is quarantined for the rest of her life.
A coup in Yugoslavia overthrows the pro-Axis government.
Nikita Khrushchev becomes Premier of the Soviet Union.
The Great Alaska Earthquake strikes.
Yuri Gagarin dies in a training flight.
Construction of the Trans-Alaska Pipeline begins.

births.text: Wilhelm Röntgen, German physicist who discovered X-rays
Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, German-American architect

facts.text: World Theatre Day was started in 1961 by the International Theatre Institute.
Washington's cherry trees were a gift of friendship from the city of Tokyo.

03-28.script:
On the twenty-eighth of March in 1592, in Moravia, John Amos Comenius was born. He believed that every child, girl or boy, rich or poor, deserved to go to school, and he wrote one of the first picture books for children. Czechs and Slovaks honour their teachers on his birthday.

In 1802, a German doctor and amateur astronomer named Heinrich Olbers found a second small world orbiting between Mars and Jupiter. He named it Pallas.

In 1910, a Frenchman named Henri Fabre skimmed across a lake near Marseille and rose into the air in a craft with floats instead of wheels: the first seaplane.

In 1941, the writer Virginia Woolf filled her pockets with stones and walked into the River Ouse. She left behind novels that changed how stories could be told.

And in 1979, a cooling failure at the Three Mile Island nuclear plant in Pennsylvania caused part of a reactor to melt, the worst nuclear accident in American history. No one was killed, but the nation's trust in nuclear power was badly shaken.

events.text: Heinrich Olbers discovers the asteroid Pallas.
The U.S. Senate censures President Andrew Jackson.
Britain declares war on Russia, entering the Crimean War.
Henri Fabre makes the first seaplane flight.
Constantinople and Angora are officially renamed Istanbul and Ankara.
Madrid falls to Franco's forces, ending the Spanish Civil War.
Novelist Virginia Woolf dies.
British commandos raid the docks at St Nazaire, France.
Radio Caroline begins broadcasting from a ship off the English coast.
Former U.S. President Dwight D. Eisenhower dies.
A reactor partly melts down at Three Mile Island.

births.text: Teresa of Ávila, Spanish saint and mystic
John Amos Comenius, Czech teacher and writer

facts.text: Czechs and Slovaks honour teachers on the birthday of John Amos Comenius, "the teacher of nations".
Pallas was only the second asteroid ever found, after Ceres.

03-29.script:
On the twenty-ninth of March in 1857, at the army barracks of Barrackpore near Calcutta, a young sepoy named Mangal Pandey attacked his British officers. He was hanged soon after, but within weeks the great rising of 1857 had spread across northern India. He is remembered as one of the first heroes of India's struggle for freedom.

In 1871, Queen Victoria opened a great round concert hall in London, named after her late husband: the Royal Albert Hall.

In 1974, farmers digging a well near the Chinese city of Xi'an struck pieces of a clay figure. They had found the Terracotta Army: thousands of life-sized soldiers, each with a different face, buried to guard the first emperor of China for eternity.

On that same day in 1974, Mariner 10 flew past Mercury, the first spacecraft to visit the closest planet to the Sun.

And in 1973, the last American combat troops left Vietnam, ending more than a decade of war.

events.text: Swedish settlers found the colony of New Sweden in Delaware.
Britain annexes the Punjab.
Sepoy Mangal Pandey attacks his officers at Barrackpore.
The British North America Act creates Canada.
Queen Victoria opens the Royal Albert Hall.
Henry Segrave becomes the first person to drive a car faster than 200 miles an hour.
Julius and Ethel Rosenberg are convicted of spying for the Soviet Union.
The 23rd Amendment gives Washington, D.C., votes in presidential elections.
The last U.S. combat troops leave Vietnam.
Mariner 10 makes the first flyby of Mercury.
Farmers in China discover the Terracotta Army.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average closes above 10,000 for the first time.

births.text: John Tyler, 10th President of the United States
Edwin Lutyens, British architect of New Delhi
Sam Walton, American founder of Walmart

facts.text: The Terracotta Army has more than 8,000 soldiers, and no two faces are said to be alike.

03-30.script:
On the thirtieth of March in 1842, a doctor in Georgia named Crawford Long held a cloth soaked in ether over a patient's face, then removed a tumour from his neck. The patient felt nothing. It was one of the first operations ever performed under anaesthesia, and America now honours its doctors on this day.

In 1853, in a small Dutch village, Vincent van Gogh was born. He sold very few paintings in his life. Today his sunflowers and starry nights are among the most loved paintings in the world.

In 1867, the United States agreed to buy Alaska from Russia for seven million dollars. Many called it Seward's Folly. They were wrong.

In 1949, the princely states of Rajputana were joined together to form Rajasthan, the land of kings, forts and deserts, and Rajasthan celebrates its foundation day today.

And in 1981, President Ronald Reagan was shot outside a hotel in Washington. As he was wheeled into surgery, he joked to his doctors that he hoped they were all Republicans.

events.text: The Sicilian Vespers uprising begins against French rule.
Crawford Long uses ether as an anaesthetic in surgery.
The Treaty of Paris ends the Crimean War.
Hymen Lipman patents a pencil with an eraser attached.
The United States agrees to buy Alaska from Russia.
The Queensboro Bridge opens in New York.
The Treaty of Fez makes Morocco a French protectorate.
The state of Rajasthan is formed.
North Vietnam launches the Easter Offensive.
President Ronald Reagan is shot and wounded.
Van Gogh's Sunflowers sells for a record price at auction.
Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother dies, aged 101.

facts.text: Rajasthan Day marks the joining of the princely states of Rajputana into Rajasthan in 1949.
Van Gogh, born today, sold very few paintings in his lifetime.

03-31.script:
On the thirty-first of March in 1889, Gustave Eiffel climbed the stairs of his new iron tower in Paris, all the way to the top, and raised the French flag. It was built for a world's fair, and meant to stand for only twenty years. Today it is the symbol of France.

In 1880, the town of Wabash, Indiana, switched on four great electric arc lamps above its courthouse, and became one of the first towns in the world lit by electricity.

In 1909, in a shipyard in Belfast, workers laid the keel of a new liner that would be the largest ship afloat: the Titanic.

In 1943, the curtain rose on a new musical on Broadway, beginning with a cowboy singing about a beautiful morning. Oklahoma! changed musical theatre for ever.

And in 1959, after a long and dangerous journey over the Himalayas, the young Dalai Lama crossed the border into India, where he would live in exile, and still does.

events.text: The Treaty of Kanagawa opens Japan to American ships.
Wabash, Indiana, becomes one of the first towns lit by electricity.
The Eiffel Tower is inaugurated.
Work begins on the hull of the Titanic in Belfast.
The United States takes possession of the Virgin Islands from Denmark.
Daylight saving time begins in the United States for the first time.
The Royal Australian Air Force is formed.
Hollywood adopts the Hays Code of film censorship.
The musical Oklahoma! opens on Broadway.
The Dalai Lama arrives in India.
The Soviet Union launches Luna 10, the first spacecraft to orbit the Moon.
The first WrestleMania is held in New York.

facts.text: The Eiffel Tower was meant to stand for only 20 years; it was saved because it was useful as a radio antenna.
World Backup Day falls on 31 March as a reminder not to be an April Fool.
